newsitem.title: USA: USDA data seen bearish to CME live cattle futures.
newsitem.headline: USDA data seen bearish to CME live cattle futures.

text.p: Larger numbers of cattle moving into feedlots in October than expected, coupled with lighter-than-predicted marketings, are seen pressuring Chicago Mercantile Exchange live cattle futures Monday, analysts said.

The U.S. Agriculture Department in its monthly Cattle on Feed Report, said cattle placements in large feedlots in the seven key states totaled 111 percent of a year ago, above the high end of analysts' estimates of 101.2 to 110.0 percent and well above the average estimate of 105.7 percent. October marketings were 93 percent of last year, under the range of 95.5 to 100.0 and average guess of 97.3 percent.

"The placement figure was not only 11 percent larger than last year it was up 10 percent from the average over the past four years - the largest number of cattle placed on feed since (USDA) began collecting data from these 1,000 head or more capacity feedlots for the month of October," said Chuck Levitt, senior livestock analyst for Alaron trading Corp.
Analysts look for December through April CME live cattle futures to trade 0.250 to 0.750 cent a lb lower on Monday.
Falling corn prices and cattle prices averaging over $70 per hundred weight in October encouraged feedlots to put 2.5 million head onto feed during the month, analysts said.
They also cited the much lighter-than-expected marketing figure for October, which may pressure December futures.

However, there was some question that USDA's marketings figure may be too low, given recent slaughter data. USDA slaughter figures showed steer and heifer slaughter down only 2.3 percent in October while the cattle on feed data implied steer and heifer slaughter was down about seven percent, several analysts noted.
Jim Robb, from the Livestock Marketing Information Center, said that even after adjusting for Canadian cattle that are slaughtered in the U.S., the marketing figure appears low.

"The risk is, that these placements could be somewhat underestimated given that marketings appear to be underestimated. If the total number on feed is right and you raise marketings, then the placement number also has to go up," Robb said.

Feeder cattle futures will take their cue from live cattle futures but may not be under as much pressure on Monday because the heavy placements of feeders leaves the number of cattle outside of feedlots at near year-ago levels.

However, the USDA's Cold Storage report, released at the same time as the cattle report, showed beef stocks down 20 million lbs during October versus an increase of 35 million lbs during the same period last year.

In other parts of the storage report, pork belly stocks came in at 16.2 million lbs, very near the average of trade estimates of 16 million lbs. Storings, as expected, were at half the rate of last year and total stocks are well below the 10-year average which should be neutral to pork belly futures on Monday, analysts added.
